 Thomas Varner: Member of the First 300 Club 
 Thursday, November 19, 2026 
 For Tom Varner, a proud member of TSA’s first hiring class of 300, the number 911 appears everywhere: on license plates, digital clocks, compliance records, U.S. currency and even cloud formations.
 Varner may notice that three-digit number more often, because the events of 9/11 had a profound personal and professional impact on him, making it more memorable.
 “I was heading to Kansas City and just crossed the Iowa-Missouri state line when the radio spilled the news about the first plane crashing into the World Trade Center,” said Varner. “By the time the third plane crashed, I had stopped on the side of the road and was at a loss for words. I just sat in my car crying and wondering what was coming next.”
 Varner found his answer in TSA, and the agency’s mission became his life’s work.
 “I recall having one thought as I boarded the bus to Oklahoma City for TSA training,” Varner said of the beginning of his TSA career. “It felt like I was headed back to boot camp. My Army memories were coming back to me as I sat on the bus with all these newbies, not knowing what the future held for us.”
 Serving TSA with integrity and loyalty, Varner has served on the mobile screening workforce; as a screening manager in Iowa and South Dakota; as a transportation security specialist (TSS) in Asia and Europe; as an explosives detection canine handler and transportation security inspector (TSI) based in Texas a supervisory TSI for North and South Dakota; and now as a supervisory TSS-canine.
 Pat-down procedures: Privacy, professionalism, security 
 An experience from Varner’s early TSA training has remained with him throughout his professional journey. The male-dominated images of the first class of screeners in 2002 foreshadowed what temporarily became a checkpoint “manpower” challenge and a memorable lesson for Varner.
 TSA’s longstanding practice is for pat-downs to be conducted by an officer of the same sex as the passenger, with supervisory or private screening options available as needed. How did the first predominantly male federalized screening force handle opposite-sex screening? As the old punchline suggests very carefully.
 Although procedures have evolved over the years, TSA has authorized opposite-sex pat-downs only in limited circumstances, not as a routine procedure. Only the FSD or a designee could authorize an opposite-sex pat-down.
 In 2014, “extraordinary circumstances” were defined as situations in which a TSO of the same sex was not available because of staffing shortages, emergencies, or limited staffing, such as at Category II, III, and IV airports.
 “I recall during the class that they put a lot of emphasis on sex-specific screening, when possible,” Varner said. “One of my most memorable experiences at the beginning of TSA was being instructed by retired Secret Service agents.
 “It was my turn to do a practical screening exercise, and my subject was female,” said Varner. “She had a very small pocketknife underneath her belt. I remember being so nervous about touching a female around her waist that I barely touched her belt line. I learned a very valuable lesson when I was told I missed a threat item.
 “Sometimes you have to think outside the box because there’s always a way around something. In this case, I could’ve asked the female subject to loosen her belt slightly and the small knife would have likely fallen out, or it would have loosened the belt enough for me to put my hands underneath it. I’ve always applied that outside-the-box thinking on the other jobs I tackled over the past 24 years.”
 Safeguarding our future while honoring our history 
 For Varner, the annual 9/11 moment of silence at the nation’s checkpoints is a meaningful observance that offers comfort and honors those lost in the attacks.
 “This holds value and meaning to me and shows respect to those who were lost on that tragic day,” Varner said.
 Varner and his colleagues from the first 2002 screener class were honored guests at this year’s milestone 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.
 “My invitation to come to this year’s TSA 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony was solely based on a decision I made nearly 25 years ago,” said Varner. “On that day, I was sworn in as one of the first 300 TSA employees to defend our homeland and our freedom. I have never looked back and have never second-guessed that decision. This is what I was here for, and I will continue to do my part at TSA in service to my country for another 25 years, so help me God.
 “Looking into the future, TSA will be an innovator for all other security agencies around the world,” said Varner. “I see TSA becoming a security giant, providing solutions to current and future security concerns. TSA will be the leading agency in counterterrorism and in developing cutting-edge technology.”
 By Karen Robicheaux, Strategic Communications & Public Affairs
